messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 31
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 42

# The Weight of Hands

Marcus is a 31-year-old Filipino-American carpenter who has been married to his wife, Leila, for four years. He builds things for a living — custom cabinetry, hardwood floors, deck frameworks — and he has always taken quiet pride in the precision of his work, the way a well-fitted joint holds without apology. That sense of solidity in the physical world is something he has leaned on his whole life. It is harder to lean on now.

Two years ago, Marcus was stopped while driving home from a job site in the early evening, his truck bed loaded with lumber and tools. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated quickly. Officers pulled him from the vehicle, forced him to the ground, and held him there — a knee pressed into his back, his face against the asphalt — for several minutes while they searched his truck without explanation. He was not charged with anything. He was told he matched a description. He drove home afterward with road grit still embedded in his cheek, and he did not tell Leila what had happened for three days.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus noticed that the drive home from work — a route he had taken hundreds of times — began to feel like a gauntlet. He started varying his path, adding fifteen or twenty minutes to avoid the stretch of road where it happened. When he passed a police cruiser, his hands would tighten on the steering wheel and his chest would fill with something that felt less like fear and more like a sudden, terrible certainty that something bad was about to happen. He began leaving job sites before dusk, unwilling to be on the road after dark.

Sleep became unreliable. He would wake at two or three in the morning with the full physical memory of being pinned — the pressure across his back, the smell of asphalt, the sound of his own breathing when he understood that struggling would make things worse. Some mornings he would get out of bed and go to the garage, where he would work with his hands until the sun came up, planing wood or organizing his tools, needing to feel like he was the one in control of something.

At work, Marcus is still skilled and still respected. His boss has noticed that he has become quieter, less likely to joke around with the crew, quicker to withdraw when conversations turn to certain topics — particularly anything involving law enforcement, traffic stops, or news stories his coworkers discuss over lunch. He sometimes loses focus mid-task, finding himself standing at the workbench with a chisel in his hand, unsure how long he has been standing there. He has nicked himself twice in the past year in ways that feel careless to him, and carelessness is something he does not forgive in himself easily.

At home, Leila describes him as "somewhere else." He knows she is not wrong. He loves her and he can feel the distance he creates, but crowded spaces — even their own living room when family visits — make him feel cornered in a way he cannot explain without sounding, to his own ears, unreasonable. He has declined gatherings with his parents and siblings more than once, and the explanations he offers feel thin even to him.

What troubles Marcus most is not the fear itself but what the fear implies. He grew up believing that if he worked hard and kept his head down, he would be safe. He built that belief carefully, the way he builds everything — joint by joint. The evening on that stretch of road did not just frighten him. It dismantled something structural. He finds himself looking at the cabinets he makes, the clean dovetail joints, the things that hold together because he made them hold together, and wondering whether that kind of certainty is something he will ever fully trust again.
